metadata.title: Premium Long-Haul Airline Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a premium airline would need to change when its hub closes, border rules change during a journey, an alliance partner leaves, or one disrupted trip combines all three conditions.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A traveler buys an itinerary operated through the airline's normal hub, meets the document rules known at booking, checks in, flies the ticketed segments, and receives loyalty credit. Partner segments are assumed to honor the same booking, while disruption recovery tries to replace cancelled flights inside the existing schedule.
metadata.residualArchitecture: Instead of treating the ticketed flights, operating carriers, airport path, border permission, customer commitment, baggage, payment, and loyalty outcome as one fixed itinerary, the adapted design keeps each obligation and binding separate over time. Network state can invalidate a route, document rules can change by segment, and partner capacity can be replaced while the same trip intent, evidence, financial record, and recovery case remain intact.
metadata.note: The tests focus on physical network change, government entry policy, alliance economics, and combined recovery. They are broader than a single delayed flight or unavailable seat.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: Volcanic ash closes the airline's main hub for five days
stressors.detection: Aviation and weather alerts, airspace restrictions, airport status, aircraft and crew positions, connection exposure, baggage state, and passenger-contact readiness.
stressors.attractor: The network's normal connection structure disappears. Aircraft, crew, passengers, bags, cargo, and airport services are stranded in different places; repeatedly cancelling flights cannot produce a coherent recovery, and protecting individual legs can worsen the whole network.
stressors.businessReaction: Declare a network operating state, stop infeasible sales and journeys, account for people and assets, prioritize protected commitments, rebuild feasible aircraft and crew rotations, offer honest passenger choices, and coordinate ground care, bags, refunds, and compensation.
stressors.residue: Separate customer and cargo commitments from the flight segments that currently fulfill them. A versioned network state contains airspace, airport, aircraft, crew, capacity, service, priority, and recovery constraints; optimization proposes a feasible recovery plan, while every affected order retains its choices, evidence, and financial obligations.

impacts.effect: Resilient operations are measured by recovery of the complete network and customer commitments, not isolated flight completion.
Operations control can rebuild aircraft, crew, guest, baggage, and cargo plans from one declared network state.
Recovery candidates expose cross-resource tradeoffs and the customer commitments protected by each decision.
Decision cycle time measures arrival at an executable network plan rather than issuance of another cancellation.
Adds network-state declaration, commitment exposure, recovery scenarios, decision evidence, and execution tracking.
Coordinates aircraft, crew, airport, guest, bag, cargo, and care recovery through one plan.
Maintains the shared disruption state, options, decisions, dependencies, and execution progress.
Optimizes feasible aircraft and crew rotations against protected commitments and capacity.
Turns the approved network plan into explainable choices for each affected traveler.
Owns the network recovery decision loop with guest, airport, crew, cargo, and finance teams.
Makes multi-hub recovery depth and transparent customer protection a network-carrier benchmark.

stressors.name: A country changes entry and transit-document rules while passengers are already traveling
stressors.detection: Government and travel-document feeds, embassy guidance, airport instructions, check-in failures, passenger itineraries, nationality and residency evidence, and rule-effective times.
stressors.attractor: A traveler who was eligible at sale or departure may be unable to board a later segment, enter the destination, or use a recovery route. One static document-ready flag becomes misleading because requirements depend on traveler, purpose, operating carrier, airport path, segment, and time.
stressors.businessReaction: Identify affected travelers and segments, explain the new requirement, collect only necessary evidence, prevent unlawful boarding, find routes the traveler can use, support documents or destination changes, and preserve why each decision was made.
stressors.residue: Represent traveler identity, nationality, residency, travel purpose, document, verification source, journey segment, transit point, carrier obligation, rule, and effective time separately. Eligibility is evaluated for each proposed path and retained with its evidence; rebooking asks the same service before offering an alternative.

impacts.effect: Trip confidence includes knowing whether the passenger can legally complete every current and replacement segment.
The traveler can keep a premium trip viable as border requirements change.
Identity and document evidence remain connected to each segment without becoming one permanent eligibility flag.
Document readiness is measured against the passenger's current complete path and rule effective time.
Shows segment-specific requirements, verified evidence, action deadlines, and eligible alternatives.
Rechecks document eligibility whenever a rule or itinerary changes after sale.
Versions traveler evidence and evaluates it against segment- and time-specific rules.
Explains the current requirement, evidence status, deadline, and effect on the itinerary.
Prevents an ineligible replacement and records the rule behind every servicing decision.
Owns reusable traveler-evidence and eligibility decisions with operations and regulatory partners.
Makes proactive document readiness across a global connecting network a premium-service benchmark.

stressors.name: A strategic alliance partner leaves and stops honoring shared itineraries
stressors.detection: Alliance notices, interline and codeshare contract changes, inventory and ticketing failures, schedule withdrawals, settlement disputes, and corporate-account exposure.
stressors.attractor: A customer bought one journey, but part of its capacity, airport handling, loyalty value, baggage path, and financial settlement belonged to a partner that no longer accepts the obligation. Treating the partner segment as an internal flight leaves the airline unable to explain or replace what was sold.
stressors.businessReaction: Stop new invalid combinations, inventory every affected obligation, secure replacement capacity, preserve or compensate customer benefits, reroute baggage and servicing, settle open money, and give corporate and leisure customers one accountable recovery path.
stressors.residue: Separate the customer order and promised outcomes from the provider bindings that fulfill each segment and service. Every binding identifies operating party, capacity, baggage, servicing, loyalty, settlement, evidence, and replacement rules; the airline can substitute an eligible provider while retaining ownership of the customer commitment.

impacts.effect: Corporate-program dependability survives a supplier relationship change without fragmenting traveler care and reporting.
Program managers keep travelers moving and can see which contracted benefits and routes changed.
Distributed offers expose the current operating, servicing, loyalty, and replacement commitments behind each segment.
Preferred-fare availability includes executable provider capacity and benefit coverage, not stale codeshare content.
Versions provider capability and withdraws or replaces affected offers across corporate, agency, and direct channels.
Lets channels sell a stable airline commitment while provider bindings and alliance relationships change.
Publishes current partner capabilities and executable offers instead of static codeshare assumptions.
Models provider responsibility, baggage, loyalty, servicing, and replacement obligations per journey segment.
Reconciles open partner settlement, replacement cost, refunds, and customer compensation without losing order truth.
Owns provider capability and controlled partner replacement with servicing, loyalty, and finance teams.
Makes accountable partner substitution and network continuity a premium alliance benchmark.

stressors.name: The hub closes after check-in and recovery requires a former partner route with new transit rules
stressors.detection: Hub closure, checked-in passenger and bag state, feasible partner capacity, current alliance capability, transit-rule evaluation, and passenger contact or assistance needs.
stressors.attractor: The original flights are impossible, the obvious former-partner route no longer carries the same obligations, and some passengers cannot legally transit the replacement airport. A fast rebooking that checks only seat availability can strand customers again or separate them from bags, care, loyalty, and financial protection.
stressors.businessReaction: Rebuild feasible network options, evaluate provider commitments and document eligibility for each traveler, keep bags and care joined to the selected path, present only executable choices, and preserve compensation and settlement evidence.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: network recovery proposes feasible paths, provider bindings establish who can fulfill each obligation, and segment-level document policy removes routes the traveler cannot use. The existing order remains the source of customer, baggage, loyalty, and financial commitments.

impacts.effect: Premium trip confidence comes from receiving an executable complete recovery, not merely another flight coupon.
The traveler receives choices that already satisfy network, provider, and border constraints.
Recovery explains the route, operator, document requirements, bags, care, benefits, and financial treatment together.
Self-service recovery counts only alternatives the traveler can legally and operationally complete.
Presents the already-validated complete recovery plan and required traveler actions.
Composes existing network, provider, and eligibility decisions into one traveler recovery.
Offers only recovery candidates approved by operations, partner capability, and document policy.
Filters replacement paths using the current evidence and transit requirements for this traveler.
Binds the selected route to explicit operating, servicing, baggage, loyalty, and settlement obligations.
Can execute the combined event through existing recovery contracts rather than a bespoke crisis workflow.
Makes complete, executable cross-carrier recovery a visible premium-network differentiator.
